tabs.label: Current Update
tabs.description: Summary of the most significant findings in the current data release.
tabs.body_html:
Current Update

July 16, 2026

The Budget Lab's labor market analysis, updated to incorporate June 2026 CPS microdata, does not provide clear evidence of labor market disruption associated with AI. Churn across occupations, AI exposure among the unemployed, and usage data all remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along pre-AI trends.

This data release completes the second quarter of 2026, allowing us to extend our comparisons of AI-exposed and unexposed workers by an additional quarter. One notable development is that the unemployment rate gap in the latest data (adjusting for the historical, pre-AI difference) has moved close to zero. On average since Q4 2022, excess unemployment for exposed workers has been somewhat positive—a pattern we do not observe for our other measures.

Of course, these findings may change as new data become available. The Budget Lab plans to continue monitoring AI-relevant trends to assess how job impacts might change.

Introduction

This interactive tool contains The Budget Lab's ongoing analysis of potential AI impacts on the labor market. Major categories of analysis can be accessed by clicking tabs towards the top of the page with the following names: Occupational churn, AI metrics, and Comparisons of AI-exposed and unexposed workers. After selecting one of those tabs, users should note the options listed on the left-hand sidebar. Those options generate different views of the data: for example, occupational churn (i.e., dissimilarity) can be tracked for the entire labor force or for specific industries.

Detailed descriptions of the analysis can be found in the Budget Lab documents that introduce each. Occupational churn, AI-exposure rates of the unemployed, and related analysis can be found in Gimbel et al. (2025). Details of AI exposure metrics are discussed in Gimbel, Kendall, and Kulsakdinun (2026). The synthetic differences-in-differences analysis of AI-exposed and unexposed workers is introduced in Gimbel, Kendall, and Nunn (2026).

AI-Exposure Metrics and Crosswalks

The Budget Lab makes use of a collection of AI-exposure metrics which must be mapped to occupation codes. The crosswalked data are available in the data download linked in the sidebar. More detail about their construction can be found in Gimbel, Kendall, and Kulsakdinun (2026). Exposure metrics are made available by Felten, Raj, and Seamans (2021), Eloundou et al. (2023), Eisfeldt et al. (2023), and Tomlinson et al. (2025). Usage data are made available by Massenkoff et al. (2026). Occupation-level data are available at both the SOC and CPS code levels.

tabs.label: Occupational Churn
tabs.description: Estimates of occupational "churn" in the form of a dissimilarity index. Interpreted as the percentage point shift in the occupational composition of the labor force. Updated monthly.

charts.title: Changes in the Occupational Mix From Recent Baselines
charts.subtitle: Dissimilarity index (percentage points). {variant} baseline.
charts.source: CPS, The Budget Lab analysis
charts.note: Dissimilarity index is calculated using a 12-month moving average of employment data

figures.description_html: The figure shows an occupational dissimilarity index for the entire labor force, calculated either on a rolling year-over-year basis or from a fixed base period. Index values can be interpreted as the percentage point change in the occupational composition of the labor force.

tabs.label: AI Metrics
tabs.description: Estimates of how AI exposure or usage in the labor market are changing over time. Updated monthly.

charts.title: Shares of Workers in AI Exposure Groups
charts.subtitle: Percent. Three-month moving average.
charts.source: CPS, Eloundou et al. (2023), The Budget Lab analysis
charts.note: Lowest, middle, and highest exposure groups correspond to the first two quintiles, 3rd and 4th quintiles, and top quintile, respectively.

figures.description_html: Using the Eloundou et al. (2023) "GPT-Beta" exposure metric, the figure shows the shares of all workers who are in each of three groups: the lowest (bottom 40%), middle (next 40%), and top (top 20%) by AI-exposure rating. Shares do not sum to 100% because some workers are in occupations without exposure ratings.

charts.title: Proportion of Tasks Exposed to AI Amongst Unemployed Workers by Duration of Unemployment
charts.subtitle: Percent. Three-month moving average.
charts.source: CPS, Eloundou et al. (2023), The Budget Lab analysis

figures.description_html: Using the Eloundou et al. (2023) "GPT-Beta" exposure metric, the figure shows the share of AI-exposed tasks within each of several unemployed groups, distinguished by duration of their unemployment.

charts.title: Proportion of Workers With the Highest Exposure to AI by Duration of Unemployment
charts.subtitle: Percent. Three-month moving average.
charts.source: CPS, Eloundou et al. (2023), The Budget Lab analysis
charts.note: Highest exposure corresponds to the top quintile.

figures.description_html: Using the Eloundou et al. (2023) "GPT-Beta" exposure metric, the figure shows the share of unemployed workers in the highest 20% of AI-exposure, distinguished by duration of their unemployment.

charts.title: Proportion of AI Usage Indicating Automation or Augmentation of Tasks Amongst Employed Workers
charts.subtitle: Percent. Three-month moving average. {panel}.
charts.source: CPS, Anthropic, The Budget Lab analysis

figures.description_html: Using aggregated Anthropic data on how AI is used by their customers across Claude and Claude API, the figure shows the shares of AI usage that are associated with augmentation or automation of work tasks. Results can be shown with observed tasks only or with missing tasks coded as zeroes.

charts.title: Proportion of Workers in Occupations Automated and Augmented by AI (As Defined by Usage)
charts.subtitle: Percent. Three-month moving average. {panel}.
charts.source: CPS, Anthropic, The Budget Lab analysis
charts.note: Occupations are considered automated (augmented) if more than half of AI usage indicates task automation (augmentation).

figures.description_html: Using aggregated Anthropic data on how AI is used by their customers across Claude and Claude API, the figure shows the shares of workers in occupations where more than half of their tasks are either automated or augmented. Results can be shown with observed tasks only or with missing tasks coded as zeroes.

tabs.label: Comparisons of AI-Exposed and Unexposed Workers
tabs.description: Synthetic differences-in-differences estimates of how AI-exposed and AI-unexposed labor market outcomes have evolved since late 2022. Updated quarterly.

charts.title: Employment Shares for AI-Exposed and Comparable Unexposed Occupations
charts.subtitle: Employment share (percentage points)
charts.source: BLS via IPUMS-CPS and The Budget Lab analysis
charts.note: Employment share is employed workers in an occupation as a share of the population in percentage point form

charts.title: Difference in Employment Shares for AI-Exposed and Comparable Unexposed Occupations
charts.subtitle: Percentage point difference
charts.source: BLS via IPUMS-CPS and The Budget Lab analysis
charts.note: 95% confidence intervals and estimated impacts are calculated according to the procedure outlined in Clarke et al. (2022).

figures.description_html: The first panel shows the average employment share of AI-exposed and synthetic AI-unexposed occupations over time, with the vertical dashed line corresponding to the late 2022 introduction of modern large-language models. The second panel shows the difference in exposed and synthetic unexposed outcomes, along with confidence intervals for those point estimates. Estimates are generated using synthetic differences-in-differences.
